-the Good-

1) A good gameplay loop , this game is effectively a hybrid between horde and extraction games . 

2) Many varied mission types , from defending a base , to exterminating everything , to rescuing civilians . 

3) Virtually no monetization 

4) this game has no classes but you can have pretty much infinite custom classes with the strategems system .

- the Bad -

1) Price . Even if the game is solid 30 dollars is just insane when you can get games like Deep rock galactic and payday 2 for like 10 and 3 respectively . 

2) Extremely group heavy even for horde standards , to the point that even if you play solo you have to be playing with random squads otherwise you basically can't win in the last 3 difficulties . 

3) There is pretty much no active teamwork in the game besides using different stratagems in the lobby and maybe healing up a teammate .

- the ugly - 

1) Crashes and random corrupts of the game just happen for no reason . Its not that bad that i would stop playing but it is bad enough to be noticeable . in my 20 hours of playtime i had to verify files 3 times already and 2 of them the game got corrupted on its own for no reason .

This is all and all a good game . all the issues the game has are directly created by the devs themselfs , all they would have to do for this to become a fantastic horde would be to even attempt to balance the game and to just have it go on sale for like 10 dollars instead of 30 . 7.5/10 i would recommend this only in a big sale . cases.claim: Reviewers report that the game becomes repetitive after playing for dozens of hours.

citations.review_text:
Helldivers 2 gameplay mostly consists of you and your squad deploying to different planets to complete operations that have the purpose of winning the galactic war and protecting Super Earth.

 You can play alone but its even better if you play with friends or with strangers in voice chat, in particular in higher difficulty missions where things get chaotic, which usually leads to insane moments where you somehow make it out alive out of a situation that looked impossible to survive. In higher difficulties it is almost impossible to complete operations by yourself, often needing teammates that are able to coordinate with you to complete the objectives. 

 The game also features a few currencies, some to upgrade your destroyers capability, others to buy stratagems, outfits and other items.

 The different factions, different creatures such as bile titans and hulks, and planets provide variety in terms of gameplay, difficulty or visuals , some planets are stunning visually, some creatures are immune to certain weapons, different objectives require different strategies. Another factor that helps in gameplay variety is the huge collection of stratagems, where you have support weapons, orbital or eagle strikes and turrets or sentries, this also provides different possibilities when facing a certain mission.

The only problem is that after several missions, even though there are different factions planets and operations, it might get repetitive, and it gets worse if you play to farm items such as samples, which is not bad, but it usually leads to very repetitive gameplay, so ideally don't stress about quickly getting everything max level and getting game items and focus more on enjoying the gameplay. 

 When it comes to performance, my specs are not very strong but i am able to play the game at medium settings with around 60fps, which is acceptable for me, if you have better specs then you are probably fine, if your system is weaker then you should be a bit more careful with graphic settings.

 Obviously this game is great, especially because i cannot talk bad about it, since it would be considered treason, and I get the honor of dying for SUPER EARTH, it has potential to create a lot of epic moments and i highly recommend you play this with friends and try out the different stratagems.

cases.claim: Reviewers note that premium currency and warbonds require significant grinding to acquire or involve paid transactions in a non-free-to-play game.

citations.review_text: Garbage game about battlepasses, without adequate implementation of paid currency being acquired for doing anything except grinding lvl 1 mission with a specific pattern of the map. Pay a fortune for the game - pay once more to use weapons that barely find their use on battlefield.

tldr: A paid game which is pretty fun but uses egregious F2P monetization. Clear potential for greatness, if only it were in better hands.

Sure, I like the gameplay. But SO MUCH of the gear is locked behind premium passes. While you can technically get the premium currency while playing, the rate at which this happens essentially means you'll have no time to play other games if you play normally. Or you'll be spending evenings here and there doing nothing but the lowest most boring difficulty JUST to gather that premium currency efficiently.

Seriously, let's do a quick comparison to Helldivers 1: HD1 has 14 pieces of DLC, the most expensive one being €4.
Helldivers2 has 22 of these warbonds/premium passes at €10+ each (2 of which cost 50% extra and give back €0 instead of the roughly €3 worth of currency the regular ones do), and counting. My primary issue isn't even the difference in quantity, it's the fact that not a single premium pass feels worth the asking price. To me each warbond is offering roughly the same amount of meaningful content as one HD1 DLC, yet they're double the price.

Additionally, HD1 DLC actually goes on sale. To my knowledge HD2 warbonds have never gone on sale, not even a reduction in price for the oldest ones.

There's also been no additions of meaningful progression besides these premium warbonds since (just checking the patch's date here) two years ago, 4th of july 2024. (I'm not counting the gun customization, it's a nice little bonus but it's also quite underbaked and has had no attention since its own implementation. Heck, they don't even properly show the stats that get changed, since the screen claims sway remains the same no matter what).

There's more issues I have with the game (performance, bugginess, stratagem bounce, biome limitations, the meaninglessness of the overarching forced plot from the perspective of a single player, unreliability of actual in-match difficulty when selecting a difficulty) but I can't really bother to go into detail on everything. Just know that it could be so so so so much better.

A $40 game with a free to play monetization model, the only progression is through battle passes and once you complete the first one that's free, you have to pay real money. Some of the best (and most fun) weapons and armor are behind these passes which is extremely frustrating since this is not a free to play game, yet you still have to pay to get them. While Premium currency can be obtained through gameplay the most optimal methods to do so are not only extremely boring, but very time consuming. It can take upwards of seven hours of grinding (with average luck) to get just a single battle pass (called War Bonds), which will only give you back 300 SC for the next purchase.

It's such a shame too since behind this atrocious pay-to-progress model, with some of the worst grinding I've seen in a paid game, is an actually fun co-op shooter. I just can't recommend it because the monetization is so greedy and so intrusive that it can really hinder the actual fun part of the game. Wherein if you want to play with some of the coolest items the game has, you will either need to fork out $10, ($15 for the legendary bonds), or grind out hours and hours of boring SC farming just to get it for free.

I’m marking Helldivers 2 as "Not Recommended" for now, even though I’ve genuinely enjoyed the game and put a lot of time and effort into it.

When the game is working well, it can be a lot of fun. I’ve been through the highs and lows with Helldivers 2 and tried to stick with it because I really wanted to keep enjoying it. Unfortunately, the current state of the game has made that very difficult. My PC meets, and even exceeds, the required specs, but the game continues to crash repeatedly.

The biggest issue is that updates often feel unfinished, and instead of improving stability, the game feels more unstable over time. It is frustrating as a consumer to invest so much time into a game for entertainment, only for it to become difficult or impossible to enjoy because of crashes, bugs, and ongoing performance issues.

I really hope the developers are able to get the game into a more stable and playable state. I would like to come back to Helldivers 2 someday and enjoy it again, because there is a great game here when it works. But right now, I cannot recommend it because it simply does not feel stable or reliable enough to play.

I anticipated, played, and repeatedly completed  Cyberpunk 2077 at release (via GOG). I even took two weeks off work to fully take in the experience on PC, using my then brand-new RTX 2060 Super. It was certainly an experience, but a mixed one. The game had various bugs and glitches and wasn't stable at all. With a little humor, I was still able to have a great time and ignore most of the technical issues.

Almost 6 years later, I gave it another try and HOLY MOLY it's a completely different game. It has fully reached the potential people saw back then. Even more than that, the developers turned it into a masterpiece.

The game can run on a wide variety of systems thanks to its highly customizable graphics settings. I tried out every setting to make it run as smoothly as possible on my build. That experience alone was fun as heck. I truly understand why this game is one of the great benchmark titles for PC hardware. It looks absolutely stunning, especially considering its age. There isn't much more that needs to be said about the graphics and performance.

The skill system seems to have been massively overhauled. Combined with your cyberware, the game now lets you create genuinely distinct builds with depth. I chose to play as a gunslinging cowboy, focused on ridiculous headshot damage and a high cool attribute. There are also many dialogue options tied to your attributes. Having certain attributes at a high level unlocks a surprising number of unique dialoge options, encouraging multiple playthroughs. In some way, this has always reminded me of Fallout NV, which is a huge compliment. I also see great potential in a Netrunner build for my next playthrough.

The story and the overall pacing are peak. I love how naturally the relationships between V, Johnny and all the other main characters develop. Keanu is a real gem and the star of the game. The choices you make genuinely matter. The world feels believable and immersive enough to lose yourself in for hours. I also love how the police and wanted system was overhauled, too.

My only gripe with the game is the long introduction [spoiler] that builds your relationship with Jackie. By my x-th playthrough, I started noticing- and hating- how hard the developers try to make him as sympathetic as possible, just to make you care even more when he dies.

Bro... I'm tired of getting my heart broken.

RIP, Jackie.[/spoiler]

It is, without a doubt, a masterpiece. Have fun playing it!

The negative review is for this: Do not buy it at full price, especially not if you have a mid-range PC like mine AND especially if you are a completionist like me. I tried to experience all the content the game had to offer in a single playthrough, which led to me "optimizing" it (meaning completing all side jobs, fixer gigs and NCPD scanners). Here is my extensive review:

Six years after its original release, I thought the game would be in a pretty great state, but it is still pretty disappointing. I think most people who praise it, they do so because they compare it to the dumpster fire it was on release. But the game still feels unpolished, even unfinished, and it's still riddled with bugs. Not game-breaking ones, but they are still there. I had to install numerous mods in order to get to a decent playable state (fix for junky melee combat, pedestrian behaviour, quality of life elements for HUD and menus, like filters etc, de-scaled skill checks which were impossible after leveling up)

Gameplay wise, the RPG elements are minimal, the dialogue options are mostly different flavours of the same choice, the combat is repetitive and the enemy AI is extremely stupid, even in Very Hard difficulty. The side content (gigs and NCPD scanner jobs) are all duplicate brain-dead quests (read flavour text, go to location, sneak/shoot, loot chest, read flavour text). And no, the city is not immersive at all for me. All the places feel the same.

Its only redeeming quality, the story and characters, are overshadowed and diluted by the immense amount of mediocre side content that continuously distracts you (text messages, calls, etc) and forces you to engage with it ("wait for a whole day until the next mission objective", "find something else to do until [character] contacts you"). 

As always, I think the level design would have benefited if was a more linear and condensed experience, allowing the player to progress through the map gradually and learning to organically traverse through the levels, instead of blindly following quest markers.

I'm considering playing it again and focusing only on the main mission, just to experience the story in a more condensed way, but I am dreading the thought of having to go through all the tedious character progress and repetitive combat.

EDIT: I played the game again, and engaged only with the main quest. It was a far more enjoyable experience for 2 reasons: 1) I was already accustomed with the in-game universe (slang, concepts, characters) and I realized this was part of why I felt lost all the time during my first playthrough, and 2) I was not distracted by the side content and I was able to focus on the story and characters).

Bottom line: Cyberpunk 2077 is a good game but its held down by the open world elements that feel they were forced and rushed by the devs, because apparently these are the minimal expectations for a AAA release.

# Kenshi — A Review

**Developer:** Lo-Fi Games | **Genre:** Open-World Sandbox RPG | **Platform:** PC

---

There is a moment early in Kenshi — maybe your third or fourth hour in — where you realize the game is never going to hold your hand. Your character has just been beaten unconscious by a wandering band of bandits, left bleeding in the dirt of a sun-scorched wasteland, with no quest marker telling you where to go and no tutorial pop-up offering consolation. And somehow, impossibly, you can't wait to get back up.

Kenshi is not a game of questlines. It's a game of emergent stories — of being a shopkeeper and a thief, a lone wanderer and a slave, and eventually an entire community of people working together to one day erect a city in the wasteland. The game never scripted any of it. It just gave you a world and stepped back.

At its core, Kenshi is an open-world RPG with real-time strategy elements and no linear narrative, set in a post-apocalyptic world where survival is brutally difficult. You begin with no skills and struggle simply to stay alive, leveling up abilities through use — thievery by stealing, combat by fighting — and slowly recruiting others to grow your band.

Eventually it becomes a surprisingly effective management game as you research technologies, construct buildings, and assign your people long lists of automated tasks — mining, farming, construction. The scope of what you can build toward is staggering. The path to get there is unforgiving.

That difficulty is the game's defining trait and its biggest barrier. The concept of a free-roaming RPG where you craft your own story is always intriguing, and the world is vast and impressive for a small indie project, but the game does a poor job of communicating its intricate systems to new players. There is no onboarding. You are expected to fail, learn, and try again. Whether that sounds like a feature or a flaw will determine whether Kenshi is for you.

At first glance it looks like a psychotic, twisted experiment. The graphics engine barely holds itself together under its many systems. There are bugs, rough optimization, and slow loading times. Visually, it will never win awards. The mechanics, however, are tremendous and extremely detailed — clearly a labor of love deserving of high praise.

What makes Kenshi genuinely special is its atmosphere. The world feels ancient, indifferent, and alive in ways most games can't replicate. Factions have their own ideologies and agendas. Cities feel lived-in. Every biome — from scorched flats to swamp-laden coastlines — carries a distinct personality. The world is fascinating, the myriad of ways to approach and play it enormous, and for those it grabs, it could easily consume all of your free time.

By May 2026, the game had sold 3 million copies — a remarkable achievement for a small studio with a niche, demanding product. Word of mouth and Steam reviews have kept it alive for years, and a dedicated modding community has only deepened the experience.

Kenshi is not a game for everyone. It is slow, obtuse, rough around every edge, and asks a great deal of patience before it gives anything back. But for those willing to meet it on its own terms, it offers something rare: a world that generates genuine legend. Your stories won't come from a writer. They'll come from the dust, the violence, and the unlikely triumphs you carved out yourself.

**Verdict: 8/10** — A singular, deeply flawed masterpiece of emergent storytelling. Brutal, beautiful, and completely unlike anything else.

Ah, Kenshi.  I purchased this game after watching numerous Youtube videos of people doing their own creative / fun "runs" (such as a slave to business owner run, or a farming run, etc).  Each looked pretty neat, and as an avid Rimworld fan I thought "Hey, this is sort of like Rimworld but in third person 3d!".  Next steam sale, I excitedly hit purchase.

Well, I stand here now having installed the game and tried it for myself, and... "underwhelmed" doesn't do it justice.  Have you ever played really old MMO's, like EverQuest or DAOC?  Imagine hopping back in now, same graphics and all, and there was no tutorial or training missions to at least familiarize yourself with the controls.  Great, I did it to myself again, I purchased yet another game where I'm expected to watch hours of Youtube videos for stuff that the game itself refuses to teach.

There seems like there's potential here, if you want a super sandboxy open world type thing where there isn't any sort of story, plot, or world events.  It does seem to be one of those "Everything and the kitchen sink, too" sort of games, where if you have an idea - you can accomplish it.  I'm just typically not that creative, and need at least SOME degree of direction  to start playing a game. 

I may revise my review in the future if I give it another try, but I fear that this may be one of those games that's going to be more interesting to watch other people play, than to actually play myself.  Maybe I'm missing something, but my brain was practically SCREAMING at me, "Now what?".

**Update with more detail**
Gave it one more quick shot since I'm a bit of a masochist / hate wasting money on something I just purchased.  I genuinely feel like I'm missing something crucial to having fun here, because both times I got dropped into the "Wanderer" start - I felt like a toddler who was abandoned in the middle of an airport; confused, lost, directionless, and perhaps a bit scared.  After wandering aimlessly around the starting area for a while, I finally had enough and uninstalled this thing.  Main issues were:

**UI / Graphics**
I am not usually against "deep, impenetrable" UI's - hell, one of my favorite games is the X-series of space games, which is perhaps the most menu driven game I've ever played.  Likewise, graphics aren't usually all that important to me, with Rimworld being my favorite game.  Despite this somehow though, Kenshi's UI is downright horrid and clunky, with buttons scattered all over the screen that go completely unexplained.  The graphics itself don't do it any justice either, with animations and models looking like something out of a circa ~2000 game (Deus Ex 1, etc).

The game very much could do with a UI overhaul, and perhaps a graphics overhaul mod as well.  Do these exist?

**Gameplay / Plot**
Biggest issue right here  - having watched folks online play this game, the thought never occurred to me that this would be a total grind-fest in order to accomplish anything.  Skills take hours and hours to level up to a level that would be considered usable, your character is utterly useless at the beginning and will fold like a cheap piece of origami.  Folks love to say that this is the point, and you "need to embrace losing" - but to be frank, that isn't really fun.  It's tedious.  I hate the whole "Losing is Fun" mentality from the Dwarf Fortress fandom, it's no different here.

Add in the fact that there's no quests, no direction, not even a vague sense of plot to really dig into.  The question I keep asking myself is "Why am I doing this?  What is the point?".  If I free all the slaves (where are they, how do I find them, who knows!), it doesn't seem to make any difference to the world, and doesn't net you any rewards.  Likewise if I make a outpost in the middle of the desert, it just feels so... aimless.  Like being the only person playing an MMO that everyone else stopped playing 10 years ago.  Perhaps there's mods out there that let me start as a "pre-built" character with combat abilities already existing, but it still begs the question of 'for what purpose?".

**Over-reliance on external material / time investment*
Posts often refer people to watch various "newbie" youtube videos, or read guides in order to properly start this game without feeling totally lost.  Some may like this, but this is a telltale sign of poor game design if you ask me; I shouldn't have to quit the game to watch an hour+ of someone explaining basic mechanics - that's what tutorials and newbie zones are for.  Please don't force me to do 'homework' just because the devs are too lazy to put in tutorials (and yes, for a 1.0 release, it's pretty damn unexcuseable).

Likewise I frequently hear "Oh, you only played 3 hours, you really need to play at least 20 to truly have it click", and again - that doesn't exactly sound like good game design.  This sounds more like Stockholm Syndrome for video games, if something isn't enjoyable for the first hour, I'm not going to waste my time.  I also loathe the fact that so many people compared this game to Rimworld, since it's pretty much NOTHING alike.  I'd say it's closer to a Project Zomboid, but with a heck of a lot more bugs and a truly atrocious UI.

**Conclusion**
Kenshi checks a lot of the boxes I love in survival / third person games - a supposedly decent crafting system, the ability to colonize anywhere, build bases, etc.  That said, this is exactly why it's so disappointing that I found it so devoid of life, bland, an absolute chore to play, and a complete grindfest.  Maybe some folks can suggest mods that fix a lot of my gripes, maybe they're "unfixable" and the problem is that I simply lack the ability to play "100% sandbox" games.  

All in all, I don't think this is for me.  This feels like an early access game that had development abandoned halfway through, they slapped a 1.0 on it and called it done.

citations.review_text:
As far as RPGs go, Kenshi’s versatility is nearly unmatched. It feels less like a game built around one genre and more like a game that keeps absorbing the best ideas from others.

Love isometric RPGs like Wasteland or Pillars of Eternity? Kenshi gives you the freedom, systems and party management you’d expect, but drops you into a world that refuses to revolve around your story. Prefer colony sims like RimWorld or Stranded: Alien Dawn? You’ll find similarly deep mechanics, except your colony exists within a much larger, more dangerous and politically complicated world. Enjoy the environmental storytelling of Elden Ring? Kenshi tells its story through ruins, scars, factions and the things you discover when you wander somewhere you were never meant to survive.

There’s a satisfying grind and progression system reminiscent of RuneScape, minus the shackles of an MMO. There’s a dynamic trade economy, faction politics, base-building, slavery, warfare, exploration and even faction creation. And if you want multiplayer, there’s apparently a mod for that, too.

You get the point: Kenshi is extraordinarily versatile. It can become the game you want it to be.

But that flexibility comes at a cost.

Kenshi does not hold your hand. Not even a little.

You’ll be confused. You’ll be directionless. You’ll get beaten half to death by starving bandits, enslaved, robbed, eaten or otherwise reminded that you are not the protagonist of this world. When you begin, you’re so weak and unequipped that even surviving can feel like an accomplishment. I wouldn’t blame anyone for falling off within the first hour.

That initial frustration is the barrier. It is also the point.

Because Kenshi isn’t interested in giving you a heroic journey. It gives you a starting condition: a nobody with no money, no power and no guarantee that tomorrow will be better than today. Your story only begins once you figure out how to survive long enough to write it.

Eventually, the confusion starts to give way to understanding. The beating becomes training. The poverty becomes motivation. The aimlessness becomes freedom. You stop waiting for the game to tell you what to do and start creating your own reasons to keep going.

That’s when Kenshi becomes something genuinely special.

It is a one-of-a-kind experience, and one of the few games that can permanently change how you think about role-playing games. Once you’ve watched a nobody crawl out of the dirt, build a crew, establish a home and become powerful enough to reshape the world around them, it becomes difficult to look at other games the same way.

Be patient with Kenshi. It may not welcome you warmly, but if you stick with it, it will give you something few games can: a story that feels entirely, unmistakably yours.

There’s a satisfying grind and progression system reminiscent of RuneScape, minus the shackles of an MMO. There’s a dynamic trade economy, faction politics, base-building, slavery, warfare, exploration and even faction creation. And if you want multiplayer, there’s apparently a mod for that, too.

You get the point: Kenshi is extraordinarily versatile. It can become the game you want it to be.

But that flexibility comes at a cost.

Kenshi does not hold your hand. Not even a little.

You’ll be confused. You’ll be directionless. You’ll get beaten half to death by starving bandits, enslaved, robbed, eaten or otherwise reminded that you are not the protagonist of this world. When you begin, you’re so weak and unequipped that even surviving can feel like an accomplishment. I wouldn’t blame anyone for falling off within the first hour.

That initial frustration is the barrier. It is also the point.

Because Kenshi isn’t interested in giving you a heroic journey. It gives you a starting condition: a nobody with no money, no power and no guarantee that tomorrow will be better than today. Your story only begins once you figure out how to survive long enough to write it.

Eventually, the confusion starts to give way to understanding. The beating becomes training. The poverty becomes motivation. The aimlessness becomes freedom. You stop waiting for the game to tell you what to do and start creating your own reasons to keep going.

That’s when Kenshi becomes something genuinely special.

It is a one-of-a-kind experience, and one of the few games that can permanently change how you think about role-playing games. Once you’ve watched a nobody crawl out of the dirt, build a crew, establish a home and become powerful enough to reshape the world around them, it becomes difficult to look at other games the same way.

Be patient with Kenshi. It may not welcome you warmly, but if you stick with it, it will give you something few games can: a story that feels entirely, unmistakably yours.

Stardew Valley is one of those games that feels like a second home. It starts as a simple farming game, but the more time you spend in Pelican Town, the more you realize there’s so much more to do than just grow crops.

The freedom is what makes it special. You can spend your days farming, fishing, mining, exploring, decorating your farm, raising animals, or just getting to know the villagers. There’s no pressure to play a certain way, and somehow even small things like organizing your farm or catching a rare fish feel rewarding.

The characters are probably one of the best parts. Every villager has their own personality and story, and getting to know them makes the town feel alive. The little events, seasonal changes, and small details make it feel like an actual place instead of just a game map.

The amount of content is honestly crazy for a game made mostly by one person. There’s always something to work toward, whether it’s improving your farm, completing collections, unlocking areas, or just making your perfect little life.

The only downside is that the beginning can feel a bit slow, and if farming or relaxing games aren’t your thing, it might not hook you immediately. Some systems also take time to understand.

But once it clicks, it’s hard to put down. It’s relaxing when you want it to be, but it can also become surprisingly addictive when you start optimizing everything.

I was very hype to get this game as was really looking forward to experiencing what others report to be an amazing game. 

Having got the game free as part of an NVIDIA promotion I have found the game to be rather lack luster.

It tackles a few genres of sci-fi, shooter, adventure rpg with horror elements. frankly I feel let down that each one of the genres lacked any real in depth playability. 

I stuck with the game for over 100 hours on Playstation (not one to easily give up before I have given a fair play but I couldn't commit any more time than this to a game I did not enjoy). Played this for about an hour on Steam to realise I was again flogging a dead horse...

The graphics were, as expected, fairly detailed and the weather effects and travel is impressive at parts. I did glitch several times even on the first mission at one point getting stuck inside of a rock to the point of having to quit and restart the mission.

I know that people really loved the fact they were playing as TWD's Norman Reedus. Personally no customisable character to associate with and a general dislike for the character model probably is the basis for my dislike of the game. 

The storyline did not inspire much emotion, it felt very slow driven for the parts I experienced. The control itself on mouse and keyboard felt very clunky and uncomfortable. On controller it did feel a little better but did leave little to the enjoyment factor.

The customisation and upgrade of items is initially satisfying but then you hit a realisation that as this is the only customisation and me not caring for the story or main character led to not really wantig to get the unique trinket idea. 

I can see where others enjoyed this but personally if I had paid more than £5 for this game I would have been furious as even felt that for a free game I wasted hours of my life waiting for any enjoyment from the game. 

Cant specifically say any 1 part was enough to recommend this, probably a bit harsh at a 2* review but for how initially it was reported this was not my thing.

A game to my knowledge that has the most intriguing opening 2 hour sequence of all time. I've made people who have no idea about game watch the opening cutscenes like as a movie night it's that intriguing. Safe to say that the story here is phenomenal. Granted the amount of story telling and reiteration of already told story is also it's major drawback.

To start I'll talk about the gameplay loop, grab packages and deliver to another location. It is basically mail man simulator. But it is no where near as boring as I swear everyone made it out to be when it came out. Maybe because I'm the type of person to grab literally everything no matter what I spent many hours just scavenging and grabbing everything and doing most side orders to try and level up each city. When doing these deliveries the environments and landscapes look stunning. It is quite a beautiful game to look at. This same beautiful environment at times is a little confusing to navigate, you can actually walk up or climb up some rocks, others you can't. This coupled with the already buggy vehicles creates some interesting traversal dynamics. Like walking will almost never fail you, but vehicles are twice as fast and can carry like 20x the loads. But sometimes the vehicles cannot handle basic mountains but the clunky climbing is still more efficient then just walking so you work through clunk constantly. But vehicle handling and terrain geometry is probably the gameplays only pitfall. BT combat and MULE combat is extremely basic yet engaging. As is trying to stealth through BT's in the snow sequence of the game.

The soundtrack fits the game perfectly, like there are some proper bangers in here. Cutscenes are voiced and acted great, but once again the sheer abundance of talking and cutscenes is the games short coming. Like the opening sequence is so interesting and "WTF", then the game begins and you are taught things. Then a cutscene rexplains what you learnt. This happens too much. The middle portion of the game is relatively cutscene free, and you are constantly fed new equipment and builds to keep you satisfied. My only issue is the last two hours of the game. Like the second to last chapter could've been done in 5 mins tops. It's a shame because the game opened so well and closed alright. It closed out the last few questions while leaving the ending open for another.

But overall, cannot go wrong with it, gameplay was fun, sometimes buggy, soundtrack was fire, graphics and visuals were phenomenal, story was 80% insane, last 20% left a snoozy taste. Atleast it didn't' feel like a rushed ending I guess.

It’s obvious that Death Stranding is a game that will strongly divide players.
You’ll either be among those who feel annoyed and bored by the gameplay, or among those who take a simple kind of pleasure from it. Judging by the fact that I recommend it, you’ve probably guessed it already: I’m part of the second group.
That said, I’ll play devil’s advocate (to some extent): yes, it’s slow and yes, it can feel a bit repetitive. As for the slow, methodical aspect, it’s clearly intentional, and I never found the game frustrating. It’s not even that laborious, really—proof of that is that I never died in the game (at least during my open-world deliveries), and I didn’t fail a single delivery.
Repetitive? Not that much, since you don’t spend the entire game in the same areas and you unlock tools that make your job easier. In fact, repetitive or not, I found the world so beautiful and immersive that I never got tired of going back and forth and exploring these stunning landscapes—it’s extremely relaxing to me.
On top of that, one thing that really kept me invested in the game was this strong sense of contribution. First with the NPCs, with whom you can improve your reputation and unlock new things, but above all with other players. I take immense pleasure in building structures and knowing that they helped other players. And it works both ways: I feel a real sense of gratitude when I come across something left behind by another player that ends up helping me. I’ve never enjoyed the feeling of cooperation in a game as much as I did here—even though it’s technically a single-player game where you never directly meet anyone else.
As for the story, I think it’s incredible. We all thought “WTF” when we saw the first trailers, and yet everything ends up being very understandable and fairly coherent. It’s incredibly original. I tip my hat to Kojima for daring to go off the beaten path and letting his creativity run free. I think many of us are happy to play as Norman Reedus, but honestly, all the characters are outstanding.
In short, whether you like the game or not will depend entirely on you and your personal tastes. It’s not a game I would recommend to everyone, but for me, it was a massive slap in the face. In fact, I don’t even have a point of comparison to say “if you like X, then play Death Stranding”—the game is just that unique.

Death Stranding was my personal Game of the Year 2019. I've completed it to 100% on almost every platform (Steam, PS4, Xbox) it's has been released on. Only exception is PS5, since I don't own one.

I absolutely love this game and consider it one of the most unique gaming experiences ever made. The world, the incredible path optimization, the emotional story, and Kojima's signature weirdness come together to create something unlike anything else.

Calling Death Stranding a "walking simulator" or a "delivery simulator" completely misses what the game actually is. Deliveries are only the foundation. The real experience is about rebuilding a broken world, connecting people, overcoming harsh environments, and helping other players through one of the most original asynchronous multiplayer systems ever created. Seeing bridges, roads, ladders, and other structures built by strangers appear in your world (and knowing your own creations are helping someone else) is still a brilliant concept.

The game isn't perfect. Vehicles can behave strangely on rough terrain, and earning every achievement requires a significant amount of grinding. Still, none of that takes away from what makes Death Stranding so special.

It isn't a game for everyone, but if it clicks with you, it becomes an unforgettable experience.

Pros:

+ One of the most original games ever made
+ Fantastic story and memorable world
+ Brilliant asynchronous online system
+ Relaxing yet engaging gameplay loop
+ Outstanding soundtrack and atmosphere
+ Incredible sense of exploration

Cons:

- Vehicles can behave awkwardly
- 100% completion requires a lot of grinding
- Slow pacing isn't for everyone
- Some gameplay systems take time to appreciate

Maxed and 500L'd this game, loved the cinematics, loved the different play modes, I even enjoyed the third person shooter dynamic though yeah the combat became less about enjoying combat, and more about satisfyingly clearing out an area for "some time" by knocking the humans out, or snipping BTs.

I went all in on developing the road and zipline networks, ending up with mostly well-maintained L3 zips; the scarcity of chemicals and sometimes chiral crystals did make this an interesting non-core, non-side-quest, non-relevant, but immensely rewarding completionist part of the game. Why drive for 20 minutes when you can zipline for 10?

Meta-game-play tip: Once you complete the game, prop your phone nearby and max Legend deliveries (or LOL) to 500 (w/sound off) while watching Whitelight's 7 hour review.

You'll get to nod your head at the critiques of BT combat, but more importantly, relive the moments you loved/liked (personal: someone hugging "themself" -- so scifi-personal I love it).

And after that, watch some No More Bikes and wonder why Death Stranding is a Walking Game With No Sidewalks!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

My gripes:
BT combat yeah, but also, why not let me clear an area and then have the sun come out?
That slippery front-end of the van.
Chemicals shortage all the time for a L3 zipline network.
Ziplines don't auto-like so I never knew if anyone used my mountain peak zips -- crucial lack of likes there.
The L/LOL 500 orders compelled my completionist compulsion.
Yeah, yeah, some of the plot/logic holes, but they never derailed me.

Final note: Much of this game is about completing jobs and building things that others can use, and both of those things are just.... SATISFYING.
